description: We are a group of students from the Dominican Republic building digital tools that help more people better understand the world around them.
summary:
SarLight is an interactive 3D globe that turns real NISAR radar data into stories anyone can follow. We built a cloud pipeline that downloads and analyses NISAR L-band scenes automatically, comparing HH and HV polarisations, and C-band Sentinel-1 for fire cases. It produces 82 cases with time series: floods across Latin America, shrinking reservoirs, drought, wind damage, landslides, earthquakes measured with InSAR, glacier flow, and farming, burning and forest clearing. Each case is set in context with population, land cover, weather and earthquake data.

Visitors explore with before/after sliders, time-lapses and a step-by-step story mode. “Why it happened” cards link each change to its likely physical cause, human drivers included: irrigation, hydropower, crop burning and deforestation. A “Is my community at risk?” tool shows nearby findings and safety advice. An AI assistant, in English or Spanish, turns the whole analysis into a conversation: it explains what the radar saw in the case you have open, compares events across countries and kinds of change, and explains the science and likely causes behind them, always using only our computed results and saying when the data does not cover a question.

Built from the Dominican Republic, a country hit by floods, droughts and storms, SarLight makes radar accessible to students, communities and decision-makers. Every number comes from real satellite data and is labelled honestly as a lead, not a ground-verified fact.
details:
What it does

SarLight is an interactive 3D globe that turns real NISAR radar data into stories anyone can follow. Our main study area is the Dominican Republic: 24 of the 98 cases are there, covering floods in Santo Domingo, Santiago, Puerto Plata, Azua and the south, the water of the Sabana Yegua, Monte Grande, Jigüey and Sabaneta reservoirs and of Lake Enriquillo, drought in the San Juan Valley and on the Línea Noroeste, wind damage in the Cibao, landslide watch in Los Cacaos and Miches, and fires in the Sierra de Bahoruco. From there we extended the same methods to the rest of the world: floods in Latin America, the US, Spain and Asia, reservoirs and lakes, cyclone damage, earthquakes, glacier flow, and farming, crop burning and forest clearing. Each case opens a panel with before/after radar images, a pass-by-pass time-lapse, time series charts and the key numbers, in plain words or a technical view.

How it works

A Python pipeline searches the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) archive, reads only the needed part of each NISAR L2 GCOV and GUNW file, and analyses it. Floods are compared with a dry baseline of earlier passes. Reservoirs track calm open water on every pass. Dated events compare the passes after the event with the normal of the passes before it. Earthquakes use InSAR phase, and glaciers use pixel-offset tracking. Each case uses the HH and HV polarisations, and two fire cases are also compared with C-band Sentinel-1 (NASA OPERA). Our home internet was too slow for this volume of data, so the pipeline runs in the cloud on GitHub Actions: adding a new event to a list is enough for it to be downloaded, analysed and published automatically. The results are crossed with population (GHSL), land cover (ESA WorldCover), weather (ERA5) and earthquakes (USGS).

Features and benefits

  • Before/after slider and radar images draped on the globe at their real position.
  • Story mode: each case told step by step as you scroll.
  • “Why it happened” cards: the chain from cause to what the radar measured to what people live through, backed by weather and earthquake records. Human drivers are included: irrigation, hydropower, crop burning and deforestation.
  • “Is my community at risk?”: pick a place and see what our analyses found nearby, how many people live there, and safety advice.
  • An AI assistant, in English or Spanish, that explains the case you have open, compares events across countries and kinds of change, and explains the science. It answers only from our computed results.
  • Classroom study guides for teachers and students.
  • Fully bilingual (English/Spanish), with a simple view for the public and a technical one for scientists.

Intended impact

We chose the Dominican Republic as our main study area because it is our home, and a country hit every year by floods, droughts and storms, often under clouds that hide them from regular satellites. The app gives it special attention: Dominican provinces on the map, the 9-1-1, COE and Defensa Civil contacts in the safety advice, and Spanish written for local students and teachers. We want students, teachers, communities and local decision-makers to understand what radar can see, where land is changing, and why, without needing to be radar experts.

Tools and technology

  • Python: asf_search, h5py, rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, matplotlib.
  • TypeScript, Next.js, React, three.js and react-globe.gl, Tailwind CSS.
  • Vercel AI SDK with free models through Groq and OpenRouter.
  • GitHub Actions and Codespaces for cloud processing; Vercel for hosting.

What makes it creative

It turns abstract radar echoes into human stories: a globe you can explore, a satellite whose 12-day orbit you can watch “dancing” over Earth, and an assistant you can ask. It connects one technology to very different phenomena, from Caribbean floods to Antarctic ice.

What we considered

  • Honesty: every number comes from real satellite data. A flagged change is shown as a lead, not a ground-verified fact, and the app shows its own cautions, such as wind ruffling reservoir water.
  • Accessibility: plain language, two languages, colour plus icons, keyboard support and reduced motion.
  • Cost: everything runs on free tiers.
  • Limits we hit: slow home bandwidth and CPU-only hardware, which pushed us to cloud processing and to downloading only the parts of each file we needed.
